title: continuous-batching-scheduler-draft-v4
content:
Summary:
This is a working draft for the continuous batching scheduler in the Redwood serving runtime. Focus areas: token-level vs request-level batching, fairness across tenants/priority classes, interaction with KV cache and kernel selection implications. This version consolidates notes from v1-v3 and contains concrete scheduling heuristics and open questions for validation in the next sprint.

Goals:
- Keep tail latency within SLO for latency-sensitive routes while maximizing GPU utilization.
- Avoid starvation / unfairness across priority classes and long-running requests.
- Minimize KV cache misses and make batching decisions cache-aware.
- Produce stable, measurable knobs for operators (batch size, max wait, token vs request grouping).

Background / motivation:
Our runtime supports continuous arrival of inference requests with heterogeneous prompt lengths, model variants, and customer SLAs. Traditional request-level batching (grouping whole requests into one kernel run) is simple but fails to utilize leftover token capacity across requests when some requests are short. Token-level batching (mixing tokens across requests into the same kernel step) improves utilization especially for causal decoding, but complicates fairness, KV cache management, and kernel selection for quantized kernels.

Design proposal:
1) Hybrid scheduler overview:
   - Default mode: token-level continuous batching for high-throughput GPU pools.
   - Fallback: request-level batching enabled per-route for strict isolation or where token-level semantics break (e.g., certain tool-calling or stateful hooks).
   - Scheduler maintains a small number of active token-buckets per priority class and model-compatibility group (same model variant + same sequence-length group).

2) Core scheduling primitives:
   - Token-slot: atomic unit representing a single token execution slot on device (logical).
   - Request-credit: a running counter for each in-flight request representing remaining tokens to decode. Credits decrement as tokens are scheduled.
   - Max-latency budget (per-request): upper bound on time a request can wait before being escalated to a high-priority fast path (preempt).

3) Decision loop (simplified):
   - Every scheduling tick (configurable, e.g., 1ms): collect available token-slots from queued requests; group by model-compatibility; assemble batches up to kernel-friendly sizes (multiple of warp/warp-group where applicable).
   - Prefer to fill kernel-optimal sizes but allow smaller batches if any request will breach latency budget within N ticks.
   - If heterogeneous sequence lengths exist, token-level packing fills shorter requests first and keeps longer requests active with minimal head-of-line blocking.

4) Fairness and priority handling:
   - Weighted fair-queuing (WFQ) approximation: maintain per-tenant/route weight and drain token-credits proportionally.
   - High-priority routes get reserved token-slots (configurable percentage) and an emergency preempt window that can steal up to X% of batch capacity if a request hits latency threshold.
   - Starvation protection: track starvation score for each queue; if score exceeds threshold, temporarily boost weight and force a compact request-level batch to clear backlog quickly.

5) KV cache interaction:
   - Cache locality grouping: scheduler attempts to co-batch requests that share recent KV cache hot prefixes (same user/session or same prompt family). This reduces KV cache warmups and memory churn.
   - Cache warmup budget: for requests predicted to be cache-miss heavy (new sessions), we favor request-level small batches initially to populate KV caches before token-level interleaving.
   - Eviction awareness: scheduler signals cache manager about expected working set size; when expected working set > threshold, we throttle low-priority batches to avoid OOM/eviction storms.

6) Kernel selection implications:
   - Token-level mixing requires kernels that can efficiently handle variable per-sequence KV base offsets, and can pack mixed-mask attention keys. Kernel selection heuristics must consider occupancy and per-sequence compute imbalance.
   - For quantized kernels (4-bit/8-bit), small batch sizes may be suboptimal; scheduler should bias toward request-level batching where kernel efficiency penalties are large.

7) Metrics and observability:
   - Per-route: mean/p95/p99 decode latency, tokens/sec, kernel occupancy, batch-size distribution, KV cache hit rate, eviction rate.
   - Per-GPU: utilization, stalls due to synchronization, preemption events, kernel selection counts.
   - Fairness metrics: tokens-served-per-tenant-per-minute normalized by weight, starvation incidents, preempt counts.

8) Operator controls / config knobs:
   - global.max_token_batch_size, global.max_wait_ms, per-route.priority_weight, per-route.force_request_level, kernel.bias_threshold, kv.cache_reservation_fraction.

9) Implementation notes / performance considerations:
   - Keep scheduling loop lock-free for common path; use per-GPU single-writer scheduling queue and per-queue token-credits to avoid cross-GPU contention.
   - Use approximate counters for WFQ weights to avoid expensive per-token calculations.
   - Ensure preemption path is rare and fast; implement as a scheduled fast-path that triggers a dedicated small kernel launch rather than killing large in-flight kernels.

Open questions / risks:
- Precise calculus for when token-level mixing harms kernel efficiency for quantized models - we need microbenchmarks across sequence-length distributions.
- How to best detect KV cache locality in live traffic without lineage metadata for anonymized sessions? (heuristics: prefix fingerprinting, session tokens).
- Deterministic fairness under extreme load: does WFQ approximation accumulate drift that matters over hours?
- Complexity of debugging mixed-token kernels: crash modes and reproducibility for reproducing mispredicted outputs.

Next steps / experiments:
- Microbenchmarks: kernel efficiency vs batch-size for float/4-bit/8-bit kernels across seq-len distributions.
- Simulation: run a traffic simulator with mixed tenants and route weights to validate fairness heuristics and starvation protection.
- Small canary: enable hybrid scheduler for a single GPU pool and instrument the metrics above; compare to baseline request-level scheduler.

Appendix: short examples
- Example A: Two requests A (2 tokens left), B (12 tokens left). Token-level packs (A,B,B,B...) allowing A to finish in one or two steps; overall kernel occupancy improves vs waiting for request-level batch of full requests.
- Example B: New session C with cold KV cache; we schedule 2 small request-level batches to warm cache, then switch C to token-level mixing.

References:

Notes to reviewers:
This is intentionally a working draft with heuristics and TODOs. Please comment on the fairness model and any missing safety constraints for multi-tenant deployments.
